title: Restoration: open L6
points: Use the six-node teaching graph. Keep the faulted branch unavailable.
Compare total restored load with restored critical load.
note: This six-node graph is separate from the voltage feeder. It represents active-power transport, not AC power flow or a time-ordered field switching procedure. Loads are picked up as whole blocks. A tie is an alternative connection that can supply load; CAPACITIES_KW sets its transfer limit in kilowatts.
caption: Six-node active-power teaching graph with whole-load pickup and one unavailable branch.

title: Choose the service goal before the plan
points: The priority goal gives more weight to two critical loads.
The comparison goal serves the most total kW, using the same network and pickup rules.
note: Critical demand totals 90 kW: 60 kW at node 2 and 30 kW at node 5. The objective is the service goal encoded as a score. The priority score gives more weight to these critical loads, while the comparison score maximizes total kW. The difference in selected service comes from that goal. Both numerical methods use the same graph, capacities and whole-load pickup rules. Neither needs a language model to solve this declared problem.
caption: Different service goals can select different loads on the same network.

title: Run L6: change the tie capacity
points: Run all of L6. MILP chooses whole loads; an exhaustive search checks its priority score.
Read served_kw, critical_kw and MILP_matches_exhaustive_check.
note: MILP means mixed-integer linear programming. Here it is a whole-load chooser: on/off choices decide which load blocks are served, while linear constraints enforce the stated network rules. Start with tie capacities of 40, 60, 80, 100 and 120 kW. The solver enforces active-power balance, capacity limits, connection to a source, no loops in the energized graph, and exclusion of the faulted branch. An independent exhaustive search checks the priority score on this small graph. Agreement supports this formulation; it does not check the AC physics left out of the model.

title: Read both service plots
points: Left: total load served in kW. Right: critical load served in kW.
Overlapping markers mean the two plans give the same result at that tested capacity.
note: The markers show sampled capacities rather than a continuous ramp between whole-load pickup plans. A higher capacity may still be too small to add another complete load block. Read both total and critical service before choosing the policy that matches the request.
caption: Reference L6 plots; rerun L6 to compare your chosen tie capacities.

title: The tradeoff at a 40 kW tie limit
points: Priority goal: 130 kW total, including 90 kW of critical load.
Most-total-kW goal: 140 kW total, including 30 kW of critical load.
note: Compare the first two output rows, where tie_capacity_kw=40. The priority plan serves 10 kW less total demand while preserving 60 kW more critical demand. These results compare two service objectives, not AI with no AI.
caption: Reference L6 results at a 40 kW tie limit: compare total and critical load served.

title: How Python checks the plan
points: Check paths to a source, capacity limits, power balance and the faulted branch.
Then compare the MILP service score with the independent exhaustive search.
note: Numerical checks and same-content evidence matching answer different questions. A record can match the inputs exactly while still omitting AC voltage, reactive-power or protection limits. Comparing the MILP score with every permitted plan is an independent check of this small stated problem. Minimizing energized branches does not calculate the number or order of physical switching steps.
caption: Python checks the stated graph constraints, then compares the priority score independently.

title: Exercise 2: add more tie capacity
points: Add 180. to CAPACITIES_KW, keeping 40. first. Predict, then rerun L6.
Compare total and critical load served at 40 and 180 kW.
At which of these two capacities do the service goals give the same result?
note: Allow one minute to predict, two minutes to edit and run, and one minute to report. At 180 kW, both methods serve 250 kW total and 90 kW critical demand. Keep 40 kW first in the list because L7 binds the first result to the first capacity. Do not reorder the list for this exercise.

title: Debrief: the tradeoff disappears here
points: At 180 kW, both methods serve 250 kW total and 90 kW of critical load.
Priority helps in the constrained case. It does not improve every case.
note: Compare the 180 kW result with the 40 kW case before generalizing. Equal service at 180 kW follows from this small graph and its demands; it is not a universal threshold. A single success percentage would hide the service-policy question.

title: Reset the capacity list, then run L7
points: Restore the original CAPACITIES_KW list and rerun L6.
L7 checks the first 40 kW record, then changes the request to 20 kW.
source_label: Classroom_Labs.ipynb, L7; cell classroom-021; request/evidence binding.
note: Keeping 40 kW first already preserves the L7 example. Resetting the list also makes the saved notebook easy to compare with the default. L7 changes the request capacity and revision without solving a new case. It tests whether the old evidence can still be used.

title: Read the evidence-match test
points: Original request: True. Changed rating with the old evidence: False.
HOLD the old recommendation and request a new solve.
source_label: Classroom_Labs.ipynb, L7; cell classroom-021; request/evidence binding.
note: This output reports evidence binding, not physical infeasibility. A separate fresh solve at 20 kW still gives the 130 kW total and 90 kW critical priority outcome on this graph. L7 itself does not run that solve. Replace the stale evidence because it belongs to a different request, even when the old plan might remain feasible.
caption: Reference L7 output: changed request, unchanged evidence, so a new check is needed.

title: Changed inputs need a new check
points: “The evidence is old” does not mean “the changed plan fails its limits.”
Update the request, solve and check it, then match the new evidence to that request.
source_label: Classroom_Labs.ipynb, L7; cell classroom-021; request/evidence binding.
note: Evidence binding asks whether a record matches the exact request, proposed plan and returned result. The diagram’s extra topology labels are teaching illustrations. The runnable L7 example changes only the request capacity and revision; students do not change topology in that cell. Old evidence is unusable for a changed request even if the old plan might still pass its limits. Ask which new numerical check would establish that for the changed request.
caption: L7 changes capacity and revision; extra topology labels are teaching examples.

title: Proposed agent role: keep the service goal
points: This cell runs Python: the operator sets the goal and limits; MILP chooses the whole loads.
A proposed agent would request that solve and explain the returned tradeoff.
note: This is a proposed role for an agent, not a new model decision in the default notebook. The current supervisor is ordinary Python. A future language-model agent could request the allowed solve and explain the returned tradeoff. It must preserve the operator’s service goal and limits, rather than quietly changing weights or making up load values. A different service goal requires an explicit new request and solve. The numerical difference here comes from the optimization objective.
caption: Proposed agent responsibilities; the current notebook cell runs Python.

title: What this model does not check
points: This active-power graph does not check AC voltage, reactive power or protection.
The energized branches do not give the order of field switching steps.
note: State this boundary clearly and briefly. The result is useful within its declared transport formulation. Actual restoration requires the utility's engineering checks, operating procedure and separate authority.

title: Restoration: Llama chooses a useful new trial
points: The new trial serves more load, keeps critical service and passes the current check.
note: Switch L10B to restoration. This is the separate L10 feeder-catalog restoration study, not the L6 six-node MILP. The recorded protocol requires a first refinement but Llama chooses between the offered fractions. SHED_075 disconnects 75% of the ordered noncritical load objects, not 75% of load kW. The exact reason calls improvement a possibility. Python evaluates the trial and finds improved service while the tie loading remains 91.867215% of its allowance. A useful hypothesis becomes evidence only after that check. This slide is a recorded preview beside the matching case. Do not run ahead to L10B yet. title: Restoration: catch Llama’s wrong ranking
points: The returned order is wrong. Python chooses the smaller cost and rechecks the plan.
note: Let pairs answer before discussing the result. Smaller cost is better, so E03 must rank before E02. Llama returns [E02,E03] while its explanation claims lowest score first. The recorded language_order_agrees_with_cost field is False. A deterministic guard retains E03 and rechecks it as E05, with no recorded failures. Human acknowledgment and dispatch remain False. The paired fixed workflow reaches the same final action and cost. This example motivates verification rather than an unsupported superiority claim. title: Restoration checkpoint: name the next step
points: At 40 kW, explain 130 total / 90 critical versus 140 total / 30 critical, all in kW.
For a changed request, keep HOLD until evidence for the current request is available.
source_label: Classroom_Labs.ipynb, L7; cell classroom-021; request/evidence binding.
note: Ask each pair to give one number and one condition.
